Reply S.p.A. (REY-IT) · Investment memo

Reply: a proven compounder priced as if its future were in doubt. Earnings growth alone should return about 12% a year, and the sector's mood will decide the re-rating.

For Richard. Written 15 November 2026. All returns are measured from the share price of €130.30 on 9 November 2026, three days before the third-quarter results; the source files hold no later price. The basis of the figures and our checks are in the end notes.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in four sentences. Reply is a debt-free federation of about 300 specialist technology boutiques that has out-grown the IT services sector for twenty years and still does. The market has halved Reply's P/E multiple on the fear that artificial intelligence (AI) will deflate IT services, while Reply's earnings estimates have barely moved. Reply's earnings should compound at about 12% a year whatever the multiple does. Whether that compounding becomes a total return of roughly 15% or roughly 80% by the end of 2027 depends on a re-rating that is mostly the sector's to give, not Reply's to earn.

The insights that matter most.

  1. The positive skew in Reply lies in the share price, not in the estimates. The shares trade at about 13x to 14x two-year-forward earnings, the 2nd percentile of their own ten-year history, on fundamentals that are intact. The scope for earnings upgrades is real but small: I expect 2027 consensus EPS to rise about 2% to 4%. Reply is not a stock whose estimates are about to be re-based; it is a proven compounder priced as if its terminal value were in doubt.
  2. Time is on the holder's side. On the model's earnings, a return to the March 2026 trough multiple of about 10x would cost about 14% by the end of 2027 and only about 1% by mid-2029, because forward earnings are about 30% higher by mid-2029. The ten-year median multiple would give returns of about +58% and +81% on the same two dates (#12).
  3. The third-quarter results were sound, not a step up, and they cooled the two upgrade levers our earlier work leaned on (the margin and the buyback). The grid below sets the results against the six tests we wrote before they were published.
  1. Reported profit understates Reply's trend by a wide margin, and the headlines have the direction backwards. Nine-month EBIT rose 2% as reported. After stripping out last year's provision release, goodwill write-off and earn-out gain, and this year's earn-out charge, nine-month EBIT rose about 13%, and the underlying EBIT margin rose about half a point where the reported margin fell a full point (#4).
  2. The buyback is the whole of our difference with consensus, and the evidence on the buyback has weakened. Free cash flow after the dividend and the usual bolt-on acquisitions leaves about €95m a year, which buys about 2% of the shares. Buying faster than that would mean running down net cash, against Reply's long habit of building it. I have cut my buyback inputs accordingly (#2, #7).
  3. Reply's earnings are predictable; Reply's share price is not. The sector sets roughly two-thirds of Reply's multiple. Reply can deliver every number and still be marked down in a sector scare, as happened in 2025 and 2026.
  4. FedTec, Reply's first larger United States acquisition, changes the risk mix more than the earnings. FedTec is growing faster than expected and appears to have cost €150m to €170m. On Deutsche Bank's account it earns a lower margin than the group, and it adds exposure to the federal budget and thin impairment headroom in the United States unit.

The five judgements that will move the value of the shares most over one to two years (the arithmetic is in #9):

1Organic growth holds near 7% and does not slip below 5%.
2The group EBITDA margin holds at about 18.2% to 18.3%, which requires Region 1 (Italy and the United States) to stay above 20%.
3Share purchases resume, at about €150m in 2027.
4Clients take back AI savings gradually at contract renewal, not in one step.
5The sector's AI discount lifts enough to take Reply's multiple from about 14x toward 17x to 19x.

What the case offers a holder: the floor rises with time, because at an unchanged multiple earnings growth and dividends return about 12% a year; the re-rating is an option whose trigger lies with the sector; and the three-year return deserves more confidence than the 14-month return (#12).

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Conclusion: Reply's operating environment is favourable relative to its sector and mixed in absolute terms. The environment supports about 7% organic growth through 2027, but its macro regime threatens Reply's multiple more than Reply's earnings.

Evidence: Reply is growing fast inside a weak sector. Surveys put growth in IT services budgets at about 2%, and European spending intentions for 2027 at roughly flat, because spending on AI hardware crowds out spending on services. Reply's organic growth nonetheless rose from about 5% in 2025 to 6.6%, 8.0% and 6.9% in the first three quarters of 2026.

Reply's business mix is moving toward the work that is growing. The Applications line (AI, data and cloud applications) has risen to 32.6% of nine-month revenue while process consulting shrinks. Regulation is turning discretionary work into mandated work: the EU's NIS2 cybersecurity directive, the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) for financial firms, the EU AI Act and data-sovereignty rules all ask for onshore, security-cleared delivery. Talent is also easier to hire: Reply's staff turnover fell to 13.4%.

Inference: Reply's growth is a gain in market share inside flat budgets, not a rising tide. Three rules that sort winners from losers in IT services now run in Reply's favour at the same time.

So what. The model's organic growth of about 7%, falling to 6%, needs no help from the IT services market as a whole. The model needs only the current direction of spending inside clients' budgets to hold.

Headwinds, sized. Headwinds are present, so topic 1 describes a tailwind with qualifications, not an absence of headwinds.

  • Macro conditions act on Reply's multiple far more than on its earnings. Interest rates are rising, our reading of the market regime is risk-off, Italy provides 49% of Reply's revenue, and Italian GDP stalled in Q3.
  • The fade of Italy's recovery-plan spending is feared more than it deserves. Reply's receipts from Italian public bodies were €87m in 2025, 3.5% of revenue, so a 30% fall in those receipts would cost about 1% of group revenue.
  • The return on AI is unproven for most clients. Only about 15% of deployed AI uses show payback, and a quarter of organisations have paused AI programmes. A client disappointment would reach Reply's revenue within two to three quarters, because Reply's contracts run 6 to 24 months and Reply has no backlog.
  • Competition in Italy is consolidating: Accenture is buying Engineering's healthcare and industrial units. The consolidation is a risk to Region 1 beyond 18 months.

Strongest counter-case. Q3's slowdown to 6.9% is the start of the tide going out. On this view, the easy comparison with late 2025 flattered 2026, the sector's budgets are being revised down, and Reply simply lags the sector by a few quarters, as it did in 2025.

What would change my view. Two quarters of organic growth below 5%, or Applications growth falling to single digits while Processes keeps shrinking.

Against the market. I agree with the market narrative that Reply is the sector's relative winner. I differ from the market on Italy: the public-funding cliff is small once it is measured. I am more cautious than the bulls on visibility: the tailwind is firm for about 18 months and unproven beyond that.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. The external forces are a share shift inside flat budgets rather than a rising tide: European IT budgets grow about 2% with 2027 intentions flat, but regulation (NIS2, DORA, the AI Act, sovereignty) turns work into mandated onshore work, and AI favours fixed-price, onshore delivery (71% and 86% of Reply), carrying organic growth from 5% to about 7%; net of the direct threats (unproven AI payback at clients, Italy's stalled GDP, consolidation in Italian competition, with the recovery-plan cliff only about 1% of revenue) this is a real but partial positive, firm for about 18 months, consistent with the group's 62 and with consensus sales growth at the 75th percentile. It sits just below Odfjell's contracted dayrate cycle and above OEM's modest Nordic recovery.

#2 Internally-driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

Conclusion: Reply's internal change is positive, self-funded and broad, but it adds up to steady earnings with a modest buyback amplifier, not to an inflection.

Evidence, in order of weight for the next 18 months.

  • Capital returns have begun, but the evidence of buying stops in July. Reply's first large buyback (an authority for up to 3.6m shares and €550m, running to about October 2027) bought about 0.95m shares, 2.5% of the share count, by the end of July, at an average price of about €88. Since July there is no evidence of further buying: management expected "very little" buying in August; the report we commissioned to find later purchase announcements found none; the nine-month report still cites the July holding; Bernstein models €100m of buying for the whole of 2026; and Deutsche Bank models a flat share count of about 37m.
  • Germany is finally turning. Like-for-like growth in Germany went from 0.8% to 5.5% to 6.0% through 2026, and Region 2's margin jumped to 16% in Q3. Fincon, the German business under repair since 2022, has produced its first quarter that looks like a repaired business.
  • The United Kingdom and France are not turning. Region 3's margin was 9.9% in Q3, against 12% to 13.5% a year earlier, because of startup costs, contractors and restructuring in France.
  • The startup engine is running hot. Reply created thirty to forty new companies in 2026, nearly all focused on AI, and won a stream of upgrades in partner status (OpenAI, NVIDIA, AWS, Microsoft). The cost of the new startups, perhaps €20m to €40m a year, is undisclosed.
  • FedTec is bigger than expected. Bought on 14 July 2026, FedTec contributed about €30m of revenue in under a quarter, against €21m expected.
  • The contractor lever has reversed. Replacing contractors with employees produced most of Reply's margin gain from 2023 to 2025. In Q3, consulting and contractor costs rose 20% while revenue rose 13%.
  • The family's control is tighter. The founding family registered loyalty shares in September and now holds 69.4% of the votes on 37.1% of the capital. The board is renewed in April 2027.

Inference: Reply's internal forces net to steady earnings at group level. The internal forces intensify a proven model and add one new habit, returning cash. Germany's improvement and Region 3's decline roughly cancel. Startups and contractors absorb whatever operating leverage exists. The buyback is the only internal force that makes EPS grow faster than profit.

Two inferences of my own that the third-quarter results support.

  1. Part of the jump in contractor costs reflects FedTec's business model, not only the cycle. A United States federal prime contractor passes work through subcontractors, and FedTec's €30m of revenue from about 400 staff in eleven weeks points that way. If so, part of the cost rise is a permanent change of mix. The comfort that Reply's headcount is growing more slowly than its revenue is then weaker than it looks: organic headcount grew only 4.9% to September because contractors, not new hires, staffed the growth.
  2. The buyback was opportunistic, and its sustainable rate is about 2% of the shares a year. Reply bought heavily at €86 to €97 a share and went quiet once the price rose above about €110. Reply's self-funded capacity is the €95m a year set out in #0. The family gains voting weight from every share bought, so I expect buying to continue, but at about that rate.

So what. I have EPS growing about 3 points faster than net income in 2027, not the 4.6 points in the model. The event that matters most for the buyback is the April 2027 shareholders' meeting, which sets the size and purpose of the next authority and may cancel shares; the October 2027 expiry of the current authority matters less.

Problems and risks. Five problems bear on Reply's multiple and on investors' confidence more than on next year's EPS: Region 3's margin; no disclosure of the startups' economics; FedTec's price and margin; a buyback that management ruled out in March and launched in April; and a closed, family-centred top team with no visible succession.

Strongest counter-case. The pause since July shows that the buyback was a one-off response to a collapsed share price. On this view the treasury shares are earmarked for acquisitions and incentive plans, as the launch announcement says, and a large United States acquisition will hand them back to the market.

What would change my view. Monthly purchase announcements showing steady buying above €120 (positive); an April 2027 authority that is smaller, or again framed around acquisitions (negative); Region 3's margin below 10% for a further two quarters (negative).

Against the market. Consensus still carries the share count from before the buyback, which is too cautious by at least the 2.5% of shares already bought. Our own earlier work was too hopeful in the other direction. The brokers' phrase that Germany and France are turning "faster than expected" is right for Germany and not yet visible for Region 3.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. Reply's own actions are positive and self-funded but net to steady: a first buyback of 2.5% of shares (now quiet since July, with a sustainable pace of about 2% a year), Germany repaired (like-for-like 6.0%, Region 2 margin 16%) and the first larger US deal (FedTec, about €30m in its first quarter) against Region 3's margin falling to 9.9%, the contractor lever reversing and undisclosed startup costs, adding about 3 points a year to EPS over net income rather than an inflection. I sit a little below the group's 63 because the buyback has paused and the offsets absorb the operating gain; between Odfjell's acquisition-and-deleveraging positives and ASML's internal measures that are dwarfed by external demand.

#3 Value chain, competitive advantage, financial profile, management

Conclusion: Reply's foundations are high quality and proven in outputs. Soft barriers to entry, no pricing power and control-first governance hold Reply back from the very top rank.

Evidence.

  • Industry. European IT services is fragmented: a specialist faces no ceiling on market share, and the industry has no pricing discipline either. Power is shifting upstream to the hyperscale cloud providers, which are Reply's partners, its sales channel and increasingly its competitors; Microsoft is also Reply's second-largest customer.
  • Advantage. Reply's edge is organisational. A partner runs each boutique, with about half of the partner's pay tied to the unit's margin, and the system has put a specialist unit at the front of every technology wave for thirty years. About 80% of growth comes from existing clients, and no client exceeds 10% of revenue.
  • Financial profile. Reply leads its named peers on the four measures shown below, and it reports no adjusted earnings at all.
  • Management. A founder family has a twenty-year record of out-executing peers through 2009, 2020 and 2025, investing while others cut. Against that record stand no guidance, thin disclosure and a board built for control.

Inference: Reply's moat is soft, but the evidence for it is hard. Nothing stops a rival from copying Reply's model, except that copying it means giving up central control, which no large integrator has done. The proof lies in outputs: organic growth 5 to 8 points ahead of peers in 2026, and best-in-class margins held through a slowdown.

So what. Reply's foundations justify paying a premium for predictability and for the record, and they explain why Reply's estimates held when the sector's estimates fell. The foundations do not justify assuming margin expansion or price rises.

A point the market under-weights: Reply's valuation premium is smaller than it looks. Reply's earnings are struck after amortisation of acquired intangibles, share-based pay and earn-out charges, all of which peers and several brokers add back. Deutsche Bank's "normalised" 2026 EPS of €8.3, against about €7.6 to €7.7 reported, shows a gap of about 8%. On the earnings basis its peers use, Reply's P/E is nearer 12x than 13x.

Four weaknesses are real. Reply has no pricing power (#5). Reply is clumsy on large bids that need several of its companies at once, and such bids matter more as clients consolidate their suppliers. Reply's success outside Italy has been hard-won: Italy and the United States earn about 78% of segment EBIT. Reply's governance protects the model but leaves minority shareholders without a takeover bid or an activist as a backstop.

Strongest counter-case. A flywheel is not a moat. If AI lets a large integrator sell fixed-price outcomes 20% to 30% cheaper, or lets clients build simple applications themselves, the boutiques' advantage of being early and close to the client counts for less, and Reply has no product or contractual lock-in to fall back on.

What would change my view. Loss of Reply's growth lead over peers for a year; Region 1's margin falling below 20%; or a large acquisition priced above Reply's own multiple.

Against the market. I agree with the market that Reply is the best house in the sector; Reply's 45% P/E premium to Capgemini shows that the market agrees. I differ on earnings quality: on comparable earnings the premium is smaller, and the absolute valuation lower, than headline multiples suggest.

Score: 65, set by the Rater. Qualitatively the structure is ordinary (fragmented, low barriers, power shifting to hyperscalers that are also rivals, and an AI question over IT services deflation) and the moat is organisational and soft with no pricing power, but it is proven in outputs: organic growth 5 to 8 points ahead of peers, sector-best margins held through 2009, 2020 and 2025, ROIC about 16.5-19% (85th percentile, on unadjusted earnings), cash conversion near 95% and net cash (EBITDA margin only 40th percentile in the Universe, a sector trait); the groups (50, 58, 75, 70) cohere with this. It sits just above Linea Directa's real but cyclical cost advantage and below Volex's certification-backed switching costs, because Reply's barriers are softer and AI makes the future less predictable.

#4 Conservatism of guidance and expectations; the record of delivery and upgrades

Conclusion: expectations for Reply are slightly conservative and Reply's delivery record is good. With no guidance and operating estimates now about right, the remaining conservatism is confined to the share count.

Evidence: with no guidance from Reply, the sell-side anchors on its own models. Reply gives no numeric guidance, sets no targets and holds no capital markets day. The brokers' models form two camps on two EPS definitions: a "reported" camp around the 2026 median of €7.66 and an "adjusted" camp near €8.2. The median sits in the lower camp, and part of it dates from July. Consensus still implies about 37.2m to 37.3m shares, a tax rate near 30% against the company's own 31.5%, and little for earn-out charges.

Reply's record against estimates is good. Revenue came in line and earnings came in ahead by high single digits over the four quarters to mid-2026, with one miss on the Q4 2025 margin. In 2024 estimates rose 22% and the shares rose 34%.

Inference: expectations are mildly conservative, by accident more than by design. Reply does not manage expectations down; it says little, and brokers fill the silence with cautious margins, which is what has produced the beats. After Q3 the brokers' operating lines are about right: my 2026 EBITDA of about €497m compares with consensus of €491m and Deutsche Bank's post-results €493m. The share count is the remaining source of conservatism.

The misreading worth knowing: reported nine-month profit understates Reply's trend. The nine-month figures look like margin compression, with an EBITDA margin of 17.9% against 18.4% and EBIT up only 2%. Once the one-off items are stripped out, EBIT rose about 13%. My reconstruction rests on broker and annual-report detail, not on the interim statements themselves.

The 2026 earn-out charge is good news booked as a cost. Acquired units such as Solirius and Graymatter are beating their plans, so Reply owes their sellers more. The charge is finite, because earn-outs expire.

So what: 2026's EPS growth of about 13% to 14% leans on the financial line, so 2027's EPS growth must be earned in operations. As reported, only about 4 points of the 2026 growth come from operating profit; about 6 come from the financial line swinging from a loss of €22m (currency losses and startup write-downs) to a gain of about €2m; and about 2 come from fewer shares. Underneath, operating profit is growing about 11%. In 2027 the financial line cannot help again (I have it slipping back to about -€6m), so EPS growth must come from EBIT up about 11%, pre-tax profit up about 9%, and about 3 points from the share count.

Strongest counter-case. With no guidance there is nothing to raise, so the cleanest form of upgrade catalyst does not exist. Redburn warns that if brokers' margin assumptions normalise, the beats will stop, and Q3's margin is consistent with that warning.

What would change my view. A Q4 margin at or above last year's 19.9% would restore the pattern of brokers being too low on margin. A second light quarter would end that pattern.

Against the market. The market reads Reply's reported margins at face value. I read the reported margins as understating the trend through the first half and overstating the problem in Q3. I agree with the market that Reply's silence deserves a discount.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. There is no guidance, which is neutral by rule; the record against consensus is good over two to three years (revenue in line, earnings ahead by high single digits in the four quarters to mid-2026, estimates up 22% in 2024 and 5% over six months, 70th percentile), marred by the Q4 2025 margin miss and a light Q3 2026 margin, and the conservatism left after Q3 is confined to the share count. That places it a little above the groups (50 and 58) on the multi-year delivery record, just below MITIE's continuing upgrades and above Renew, which did cut.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost control and feedback loops

Conclusion: Reply's business model offers resilience, not amplification. Outsized EPS growth comes only from the buyback, and investors should not underwrite a margin breakout.

Evidence.

  • Pricing power: none shown. Revenue per employee is flat at about €153,000 while salaries rise about 3.5%. Reply has held its margin through mix and productivity, not through price.
  • Operating leverage: low and capped. About 80% of Reply's costs flex within a year, so two points of extra organic growth move the EBITDA margin by only 0.3 to 0.6 point. Contractors, at about half the gross margin of employees, staff faster growth first, which is what Q3 showed.
  • Financial leverage: negative. Net cash including leases was €397m at the end of September, after paying for FedTec.
  • Cost control: a defensive lever, not an offensive one. Slowing startup creation, freezing graduate hiring and the automatic fall in partner pay protect 1 to 1.5 points of margin in a downturn.
  • Feedback loops. Reinforcing loops drive revenue, and balancing loops cap the margin (shown below).

Inference: Reply turns revenue growth into profit growth at about one for one, not more. The honest answer to topic 5's question is that Reply's business model does not amplify growth; Reply's balance sheet does. The model's EPS growth of 10% to 14% on revenue growth of 7% to 9% is therefore revenue growth plus the buyback, with almost nothing from margin.

So what. Value Reply's growth as it is: about 8% revenue growth passed through to profit at the same rate, plus whatever cash is returned. An investment case that needs margins to rise is a different case from this one.

The asymmetry to hold in mind. The contractor loop caps the upside leverage. Downside protection is thinner than in 2025, because contractors are now about 17% to 18% of revenue, against about 27% in 2023, so there is less to cut. And one loop can turn: if clients bank their AI savings and stop reinvesting them, the loop that now drives volume becomes a drag on price (#9, judgement 4).

Strongest counter-case (the bull's). Fixed-price work plus AI is latent operating leverage: delivery effort falls by up to 30% while the contract price holds. If Reply keeps even a third of that saving beyond renewal, or moves toward outcome-based pricing as Netcompany has, Reply's margin breaks out of the 18% band.

What would change my view. A first disclosure of AI productivity kept after contract renewal, or Region 1's margin holding at 21% or more with FedTec inside it.

Against the market. I agree with Bernstein that Reply's operating leverage is limited. I do not agree that Reply's margins are at a structural peak: Germany's repair and maturing startups are worth 0.3 to 0.5 point over three years, which is why my margin path drifts up from 18.2% to 18.6% and does not fall.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. The structure barely amplifies: no pricing power (revenue per head flat while pay rises 3.5%), about 80% of costs flex within a year so two points of growth move the margin only 0.3 to 0.6 point, faster growth is staffed by lower-margin contractors, and net cash means no financial leverage, so profit grows about one for one with revenue and only the buyback (about 1.6% of EPS per €100m) adds; consensus EPS growth of 7.9% against sales growth of 7.3% (32nd and 75th percentiles) confirms the low ratio. The economic-strength group's 75 reflects returns and cash, not gearing; I place it above the 25 level only for the buyback optionality from net cash and the latent fixed-price AI productivity the memo cannot yet evidence.

#6 Forecast financials

Conclusion: the forecasts offer four years of 10% to 14% EPS growth, built on about 8% revenue growth and a modest buyback. That profile is steadier but slower than Reply's past.

What would change my view. Q4 organic growth below 6%, or a Q4 margin more than a point below last year's, would take 2027 EPS toward €8.1 to €8.3, about level with consensus.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. Growth in the 10-15% band gives B; I place it low in the band because revenue growth roughly halves from 13% a year to about 8%, the margin is flat against a four-point rise in the past, part of 2026-27 growth is the financial line swing, the FedTec acquisition and the buyback, and consensus is lower (7.9% next year, 32nd percentile).

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and narrative over 6 to 12 months

Conclusion: upgrades to Reply's estimates are likely but small, around 2% to 4% for 2027. The more visible upgrading will come through brokers' target multiples and the narrative, not through earnings.

Guidance: none exists, and I put the chance of Reply introducing any at under 10%. The nearest equivalents are the April 2027 buyback authority, which I think about 80% likely to be renewed, and management's tone. Deutsche Bank read management's tone after Q3 as pointing to reported growth near double digits over the next 18 months, which is above consensus revenue growth of about 8% for 2027.

Estimates: 2027 consensus EPS (€8.33) is likely to rise about 2% to 4%, and the shares already bought are the largest single source of the rise.

The first evidence fits that estimate: after the Q3 results Bernstein raised its 2027 EPS by about 1%, and Deutsche Bank left its numbers broadly unchanged. The largest single step should come in mid-March 2027, when Reply reports its year-end share count.

So what. Estimates should drift up, which supports the shares and keeps Reply at the top of its sector for revisions. The upward drift in estimates is too small to carry a re-rating by itself.

Narrative: the brokers' post-Q3 notes raised target prices through higher multiples, not higher earnings. Analysts cut their targets by cutting multiples on the way down, and they are now reversing those cuts. Rising target multiples are the form the narrative upgrade is taking, and that upgrade can run further.

What would make the narrative step up. Bernstein's stated bar for multiple expansion is organic growth comfortably above 5%, with Regions 2 and 3 contributing; Germany (Region 2) now contributes. The most powerful change available, and the least likely, is a first disclosure by Reply of AI productivity or of pricing at contract renewal. A resolution to cancel shares at the April 2027 meeting, which I put at about 15% likely, would be the nearest thing to a guidance upgrade.

Strongest counter-case. Upgrades of 2% to 4% are too small to drive a share price that has already risen 42% in six months. With 92% of brokers at Buy, the next rating changes are more likely to be downgrades than upgrades. A French goodwill write-off at the year-end would also cut reported EPS (#9).

What would change my view. Resumed monthly buying would add 2 to 3 points to the upgrade path for 2028 EPS. Q4 organic growth below 6% would turn the net 2027 upgrade to about zero.

Against the market. The sell-side has the direction of revisions right and their size about right. The sell-side has not yet modelled the shares already bought, and that part of the upgrade is close to certain. Our earlier claim that EPS would come in 6% and 10% above consensus was too high.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. No guidance to raise (under 10% chance of any), though management's tone points to reported growth near double digits against about 8% in consensus; 2027 consensus EPS should rise about 2% to 4% (stale July models, FedTec's true size and the 2.5% of shares already bought, less tax and earn-out charges), which against revenue growth of about 8-9% is a ratio of roughly 0.3 to 0.45, near the 60th percentile, and the narrative is improving through target multiples, capped by 92% of brokers already at Buy. The group's 57 agrees; this is a little below Teqnion's upward pressure from a trough and above Spie's flat revisions with a raised target.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, share price, and peers

Conclusion: Reply's momentum is strong in the share price, positive but slowing in estimates, absent in guidance and weak in the sector theme. That combination is what the early stage of a quality-led sector recovery looks like.

Evidence (dashboard readings of 6 to 9 November; none is mine to alter).

  • Sell-side. Consensus 2027 EPS is up 6% over six months but only 1% over three months; target prices are up 5%; and 92% of brokers rate the shares Buy. Sell-side momentum is rated B, and Reply's revision score of 14 is the highest of the eighteen stocks in its sector.
  • Price. Technical momentum is rated A. The shares are up 42.5% in six months, about 70% above their 52-week low and at the 86th percentile for relative strength. The shares are 26% above a 200-day moving average that has been rising for only three months.
  • Theme. Thematic momentum for the IT services sector is rated D.
  • Peers. Twelve of the seventeen peers are now rated A or B for technical momentum, but none is rated above C for earnings momentum, and nine are rated A for valuation.
  • Guidance. Reply gives none.

Inference: Reply is the only stock in its group where both the share price and the estimates confirm a recovery. The sector's share prices are recovering ahead of its earnings, as they did after 2009. Reply's profile is that of a leader early in a sector recovery. It is also the profile of a stock that has already taken the easy part of the move: about 34 of the 42 points of six-month price gain came from a higher multiple, not from higher earnings.

So what: momentum supports the case but is not, on its own, a reason to own the shares. The shares are stretched against their trend: a fall of 15% to 20% to the 150-day or 200-day moving average would be unremarkable and would not break the uptrend. The dashboard P/E read 13.1x on both 8 and 13 November, which suggests that the Q3 results did not move the share price much.

Strongest counter-case. A stock rated A for momentum inside a theme rated D is a divergence that usually closes one way or the other. If the sector's estimates keep falling (Capgemini's book-to-bill ratio is at its lowest since 2020), Reply's valuation premium is exposed.

What would change my view. Peers' earnings momentum turning up to B would show the recovery broadening beyond Reply and would support the re-rating. Reply's revisions turning negative over three months would show the sector leader stalling.

Against the market. No difference: the dashboard readings are the market. I would add only that the three-month pause in revisions deserves more attention than the six-month gain.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. Both measures positive and none strongly negative gives B; I place it low in the band because the sell-side reading is only just above neutral (three-month EPS revision 0%, 45th percentile, against +5% over six months, 70th), there is no guidance, and peers' earnings momentum is weak (which does not pull the letter down), while the price is strong (up 42% in six months, 26% above a rising 200-day average) and target prices are being raised.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts

Conclusion: Reply's forecasts are simple and low-risk down to EBITDA and noisy below it, while Reply's share price carries a sector-driven multiple risk several times larger than any plausible earnings miss.

How simple is the case? Simple down to EBITDA, opaque from EBITDA to EPS. Down to EBITDA, the forecast is headcount times revenue per head, a cost base that flexes, and three regions. From EBITDA to EPS, earn-out re-measurement, write-downs, currency, tax and the share count hold most of the surprises; the company does not explain these items, and they tripped up two of our own earlier sets of work. Reply's reported lines need three adjustments at every set of results (provisions, the gap between EBITDA and EBIT, and currency) before they mean anything.

The range of likely EPS outcomes is narrow for 2026, wider for 2027 and skewed down. For 2026, with nine months reported, EPS is within about 2% either way of my centre. For 2027 I see a range of about -12% to +6% around my centre, at roughly 80% confidence, and operations account for two-thirds of the width of that range. The 2027 range is skewed down in size, because balancing loops cap the upside and write-downs cost money whether acquired units do well or badly. The large downside outcomes are unlikely, however, and flexible costs, net cash and a buyback that speeds up at lower prices cushion them.

The five judgements, with the arithmetic. The base is 2027 on the company's basis after my input changes, rounded, in € millions: revenue 2,980; EBITDA 545; EBIT 452; pre-tax profit 446; net income 308; 35.7m average shares; EPS about €8.63. The percentage effects apply equally to the model's figures.

Judgement, and how it could be wrongArithmetic (€ millions)Effect on EPSWhat else follows
1. Organic growth holds near 7%. Wrong by two points lower from Q4 2026 through 2027, a repeat of 2025.Revenue about -15 in Q4 2026 and about -2.3% in 2027: -68, to about 2,911. Margin -0.45 point to 17.85% (the rule of 0.3 to 0.6 point per two points of growth). EBITDA 2,911 x 17.85% = 520: -26 (-4.7%). EBIT -26 (-5.7%). Net income -26 x 0.69 = -18, to 290.290 / 35.7 = €8.13: -€0.50 (-5.8%)Free cash flow about unchanged, because €68m less revenue releases about €19m of working capital (28% of revenue). Value -6% at any given multiple. The larger effect: growth below 5% is Bernstein's stated condition for no re-rating.
2. The EBITDA margin holds at about 18.3%. Wrong by half a point.EBITDA 2,980 x 0.5% = -15 (-2.7%). EBIT -15 (-3.3%). Net income -10. Free cash flow -10.-€0.29 (-3.3%)The concentrated version: one point of margin in Region 1 (Italy and the United States, about 1,960 of revenue) is about -20 of EBITDA and -4.3% of EPS, more than the whole of the regional repair in the forecast.
3. Share purchases resume at about €150m in 2027. Wrong by none at all, or by full use of the authority.No further buying: the count stays at 36.33m; 2027 EPS = (308 + 1.5 of extra interest) / 36.33 = €8.52. Full use of the cap by October 2027: about 2.5m more shares.None: -1.3% in 2027, -3.5% in 2028. Full: about +1.6% in 2027, about +2.8% in 2028.The range in 2028 EPS is about six points wide, and each 0.5m shares is 1.4%. Net cash moves the other way: roughly +€165m (no buying) or -€175m (full use) by the end of 2027.
4. Clients take back AI savings gradually. Wrong by organic growth one point a year lower from mid-2027 because of price, with no matching fall in cost.Revenue -15 in 2027 (half a year), about -48 in 2028 and about -85 in 2029, as the shortfall compounds. Drop-through about 75% after the automatic fall in partner pay, high because the delivery effort has already been taken out. EBIT -11 in 2027, -36 in 2028, -64 in 2029.-2.5% in 2027, about -7% in 2028, about -12% in 2029This outcome would prove the sector's AI discount right, so it would cost the multiple as well as the earnings. It cannot be observed before the first-half 2027 results in late July 2027.
5. The sector's AI discount lifts. Wrong by any amount; this judgement has the widest range.On the model's two-year-forward EPS at the end of 2027 (€10.83), each turn of P/E is €10.8 a share, 8.3% of today's price.None; the effect is on the priceShare price at end-2027: €108 at the March 2026 trough of about 10x; €150 flat at 13.8x; €203 at the ten-year median of 18.7x; €234 at the guideline of 21.62x.

Being wrong on judgements 1 to 4 all at once would move EPS by roughly 15%. Being wrong on judgement 5, the multiple, would move the share price by 50% or more.

So what: size the risk in Reply on the multiple, not on the earnings. The earnings judgements are each worth a few percent and can be tracked quarter by quarter. The multiple is worth half the share price and moves on other companies' news.

Cyclicality and trackability: Reply's record through downturns is resilient, but nothing Reply publishes warns of the next one. Reply's revenue was flat in 2009 with the margin down 1.3 points; revenue grew 5.7% in 2020; and Reply's one year of falling EPS (-2%) came in 2023, when growth halved after a hiring wave. Changes in demand reach Reply's revenue within two to three quarters, and Reply publishes no backlog or order intake that would warn in advance. The case can therefore be monitored but not anticipated.

Sudden and sentiment risks, from the sector's own history. IT services multiples collapsed in 2003, 2009, 2020 and 2025 to 2026, and recovered each time where delivery held, usually before revenue turned. The companies that failed did so for different reasons, and Reply carries none of those weaknesses:

Cause of failureExample in the sectorReply
A hiring wave into falling utilisationAdesso: margin down to 2.7% in a quarterNot present
Hourly billing and offshore deliveryNagarroNot present: 71% fixed-price, 86% onshore
LeverageAtosNot present: net cash
Inflated adjusted earningsGlobant, EndavaNot present: no adjusted earnings reported

Reply's own risk list is shorter and more specific:

  • A sector AI scare or a peer's profit warning could take four points off Reply's multiple, 25% to 30% of the price, within weeks, whatever Reply reports. Capgemini's €2bn buyback did not stop its multiple falling from 11x to 8x in early 2026, so a buyback is no defence against this risk.
  • A goodwill write-off at the March 2027 results, most likely in France. At the end of 2025 the French unit's impairment headroom was 10% on €69m of goodwill, and the impairment test fails on a half-point rise in the discount rate; market rates have risen since. I put about one in three on a charge at one of the next two year-ends. A €20m charge would take about 7% off reported EPS for the year, with no cash effect and no effect on adjusted EPS. Our earlier work looked for this write-off in Germany, where headroom is ample.
  • The United States unit: its impairment headroom was 40% before FedTec; both main brokers describe the existing United States business as a drag; and federal funding runs on a stopgap to 11 December 2026.
  • Italian sovereign stress would hit the half of Reply's revenue earned in Italy and Reply's multiple together.

Strongest counter-case to "earnings are low-risk". Reply built its record of resilience with a contractor buffer that is now mostly spent, in years before AI gave clients a reason to reopen prices. The next slowdown would be the first test of Reply's model without either protection.

What would change my view. Any of the three signals that would move my central forecast: organic growth below 4% to 5% for two quarters; Region 1's margin below 20% for a half-year; or no share purchases by the March 2027 results.

Against the market. The market prices the AI question as a risk to Reply's terminal value. I price it as a risk of about 7% to EPS by 2028 and 12% by 2029 if it goes wrong. Both views can be right: the multiple is paying for uncertainty that only time removes.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. Operations are simple and buffered (2026 EPS within about 2%, a flexible cost base, net cash, revenue flat in 2009 and only one down EPS year), but the 2027 cone is about -12% to +6% at 80% confidence and skewed down, the lines below EBITDA (earn-outs, write-downs, currency, tax, share count) are opaque, there is no backlog to warn in advance, and the share price carries a sector-driven multiple that can lose 25-30% within weeks, plus a one-in-three French goodwill charge, FedTec's federal funding and Italian sovereign exposure. The groups (50 and 64) bracket this; it sits just below Shell's resilient but price-exposed case and above Nexans' lumpy project timing.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: Reply is early in the Broadening phase. The stock has turned and the thesis is widening, but upgrades are small, and the next phase depends on evidence that the sector, not only Reply, must supply.

The dashboard's rule places Reply in the "Broadening" phase. I agree, with the qualifier "early".

Inference: the remaining thesis is a valuation thesis. Reply's thesis has broadened from "Reply is not dying" to "Reply is the sector's winner". The thesis has not reached "Reply's earnings power is stepping up", and on our forecasts it will not. The thesis that remains is "the market's discount was wrong", which is a valuation thesis and needs evidence from the sector.

So what. A stock early in Broadening still has most of its re-rating ahead of it if the evidence keeps arriving, and Reply has not yet earned a peak-phase multiple (#11).

What moves Reply on to the next phase, and what moves it back.

  • To Reinforcing: two more quarters of organic growth of 7% or more with margins up year on year, purchases resumed, and peers' estimates turning up.
  • To Stalling: organic growth of 5% or less, a second margin slip, or silence on the buyback through the March 2027 results.

Strongest counter-case. After a rally of about two-thirds driven by the multiple alone, and with growth just off its high, the share price is at the top of a relief rally, not at the start of a broadening.

Against the market. The price action says Reply is broadening; the sector theme says not yet. I side with the price, on the evidence of Reply's delivery, but I would not call the current phase one of peak delivery.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. The stock has turned up and the cause for concern is clearing (growth back to about 7%, Germany inflected, AI fears contradicted by three quarters, targets being raised through multiples), so the memo's early Broadening is fair and ahead of the computed Turning/Inflecting, but forecasts show no acceleration in growth or margin, revisions have paused over three months, Q3 decelerated slightly and a 42% rally has taken the easy part. It sits between Kuehne + Nagel's early Reinforcing on a raised guide and Tenaris' Reinforcing with an uncertain upturn.

#11 The fair multiple

Conclusion: the guideline P/E of 21.62x is defensible as a destination but early as a target for the end of 2027. By then, Reply's own delivery can earn about 17.5x to 19x.

The guideline: 21.62x two-year-forward earnings, far above every current reading. Viewforth's rule gives 21.62x for a stock in Broadening, the 80th percentile of Reply's ten-year history. The guideline is 65% above the dashboard's 13.1x today and 57% above the 13.8x the model computes on our own earnings. FactSet's weekly series reads 14.6x, the 22nd percentile of five years. The three readings differ in the earnings they divide by, but all three put the shares near the bottom of their range.

My view: 21.62x is a fair price for Reply in a normal sector mood, and too much to ask by the end of 2027.

For the guideline. Through 2024 and into early 2025 the market paid 19x to 21.5x for Reply when revenue was growing 8% to 9% and EPS 14% to 16%, a profile very close to today's. The business has not deteriorated since then; if anything, Reply's relative position has improved. The guideline therefore does not need a return to the boom.

Against the guideline, for now.

  1. History. In the 120 month-ends of history, Reply closed at or above 21.62x in 25, and every one of those 25 fell between May 2020 and July 2022, the zero-rate digital boom. Outside that window Reply's P/E touched 21.5x twice and never held the guideline level.
  2. Rates and the AI question. Interest rates are higher now than in 2024, and the AI question has been asked. Reply's results alone will not un-ask that question, because about two-thirds of Reply's multiple is set by the sector.
  3. Sequence. The evidence that would justify clearing the discount in full is pricing at contract renewal, which first shows in the half-year results of late July 2027 and properly in 2028. The model reaches the guideline on 31 December 2027, before most of that evidence exists.
  4. Phase. Viewforth's rule gives higher multiples to the phases of peak delivery. I read the stock as early in Broadening, which argues for a multiple in the middle of the historical range, not at the 80th percentile.

What I would underwrite: 17.4x to 18.7x by the end of 2027. Those are the dashboard's "conservative" and "prudent" bands; the latter is the ten-year median. Reply's own delivery can plausibly earn that multiple if growth holds. By mid-2029, with the renewal cycle visible, the guideline becomes reachable. Topic #12 uses the guideline as instructed, and I give the other multiples beside it so that the return's dependence on the multiple is plain.

Strongest counter-case to my caution. Multiples lead fundamentals: after 2009 and 2020 the sector re-rated before revenue turned, and Deutsche Bank has already moved its target multiple up a turn on one quarter's results. A market that decides the AI fear was wrong will not wait for the 2028 accounts.

What would change my view. Upward: peers' estimates turning up, and a Reply disclosure on renewal pricing. Downward: organic growth below 5%, at which point 14x to 15x is fair and the guideline is out of reach.

Against the market. The market's multiple says Reply's terminal value is in doubt. I think the market is too harsh for a business with Reply's record and balance sheet, and that the guideline is too generous on timing. The fair answer for the next 14 months lies between the two, nearer the ten-year median.

Score: 91, set by the Rater. Cheap on both gives A; I place it near the floor because part of the cheapness is deserved: the ten-year history includes the 2020-22 zero-rate boom and a faster-growing Reply (13% revenue growth against about 8% ahead), rates are higher, the AI question is sector-wide, and the cohort is only three stocks, though on peers' adjusted-earnings basis the shares are cheaper still.

#12 Total shareholder return

Conclusion: the return at the guideline multiple is +82% to the end of 2027 and +109% to mid-2029. Only the earnings and dividend part, about 12% a year, is within Reply's control; the rest is a re-rating I would count on more over three years than over 14 months.

The model's return at the guideline fair multiple (from €130.30; the model was built before Q3):

HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedFrom earningsFrom the multipleFrom dividends
To 31 December 2027 (the model's 18-month column; about 14 months from the price date)+82.2%+69.5%+14.5%+56.9%+2.5%
To 30 June 2029 (the three-year column; about 2.6 years)+108.8%+32.2%+30.5%+56.9%+4.0%

The three parts do not add up to the total: the earnings and multiple parts multiply, and dividends add.

What drives each part of the return.

  • Earnings (+14.5% to end-2027, then +30.5% to mid-2029): the part Reply controls. The two-year-forward EPS rises from about €9.45 today to €10.83 at the end of 2027. That rise is net income growing 8% to 9% a year (revenue up about 8%, margin about flat) plus about 3 points a year from the share count in the model. Our third set of work found this part of the return predictable.
  • The multiple (+56.9% at both horizons): the part Reply does not control. The model takes the P/E from 13.8x to 21.62x, reached at the end of 2027 and held. The multiple supplies 69% of the first return and about half of the second.
  • Dividends (+2.5%, then +4.0%). Reply pays out about 20% of earnings, a yield just over 1%. Cash returned through the buyback sits in the earnings part.

The same earnings at other multiples: the chart I would look at first.

If earnings also fall short, in a bear case about 12% below the model, the trough multiple gives about -25% at the end of 2027 and about -13% by mid-2029.

Reading the chart.

  1. The floor rises with time. At an unchanged multiple the shares return about 12% a year from earnings growth and dividends, and even a full retest of the trough multiple is recovered by mid-2029. A rising floor is what a compounder bought at a low multiple offers, and the rising floor is the positive skew in the case.
  2. The re-rating is an option with a sector trigger. My rough odds for the multiple at the end of 2027 are shown below. They centre on about 16x and a return of about +35%, with the range of outcomes above that centre. These odds are judgements, offered so that the shape of the outcomes is explicit, not as precision.
  3. The two horizons deserve different confidence. I would lean on the three-year figure more than on the 18-month figure. The guideline is more plausible once the renewal evidence exists (#11), and by mid-2029 earnings supply half the return.

Effect of my input changes: the guideline return to end-2027 falls from about +82% to about +76%. My EPS, about 3% lower than the model's from 2027, leaves the earnings part unchanged at about 14.5% but lowers the multiple part to about +52%, because the same share price on lower earnings is a higher starting multiple. The updated model will give the exact figures.

Strongest counter-case. The whole upper half of the chart assumes the sector discount lifts within 14 months. If the discount does not lift, the realistic outcome is the 13.8x case, which is a good return but not the one in the headline.

What would change my view. The triggers for the multiple are in #11 and the triggers for earnings are in #9.

Against the market. Brokers' targets after Q3 (€147 to €171.5) imply returns of about +13% to +32% over twelve months, close to my centre and well below the guideline return. I agree with the brokers' centre and think they understate the three-year compounding.

Score: 84, set by the Rater. About +32% sits high in the B band (20-35%); I hold it at 84 rather than 87 because most of the return rests on a sector re-rating Reply does not control and the lower tail reaches -14% to -25% at the trough multiple, while the three-year check is supportive (about +35% at an unchanged multiple, about 12% a year from earnings and dividends).

#13 Summary conclusion

Reply is a high-quality, cash-rich, founder-run compounder whose shares were de-rated for a risk that its own results have so far contradicted. The business will very probably deliver earnings growth of 10% to 14% a year through 2028 from gains in AI, data and regulated work, flexible costs and a modest buyback. Reply needs no pricing power, no margin breakout and no further large acquisition to deliver that growth.

Why the case is attractive
  • The starting multiple is at the bottom of a ten-year range.
  • Earnings growth alone gives about 12% a year.
  • The downside to the tested trough multiple is about 14%, and it shrinks with time.
  • Any easing of the sector's AI discount adds 30 to 65 points of return.
Why the case is limited
  • Nothing in Reply's own gift is unusually skewed.
  • Upgrades are a few percent.
  • Margins are flat.
  • The buyback has paused.
  • The multiple is mostly the sector's.

The third-quarter results fit that reading. Growth is intact, Germany is repaired and FedTec is bigger than thought; the margin was lighter, earn-out charges recur and the buyback is unconfirmed. I have trimmed the forecast inputs, not the thesis.

What to watch is short and observable.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 62, set by the Rater. Clearly positive but partial input forces (external 60, internal 60) reach profits surely but only at about the Universe's median growth (EPS about 11-12% a year, a B on Richard's cut-offs but with a flat margin and growth halving from the past), so the net change is a mild positive in the low 60s, not a step-up, which agrees with the memo's C.

Foundations' Robustness: 68, set by the Rater. Quality of 65 rests on a soft, organisational moat in a fragmented industry facing the AI deflation question, but robustness is lifted by what made it resilient for twenty years (sector-best margins held through 2009, 2020 and 2025, ROIC at the 85th percentile on unadjusted earnings, net cash, capital-light, no client above 10%) and a good delivery record against consensus (62); no pricing power and control-first governance keep it below the 75 band and the memo's B.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 74, set by the Rater. The case fits the memo's setup, cause for concern clearing in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business on a bottom-quartile multiple, in nearly every element (proven quality, multiple at the 2nd percentile, AI fear contradicted by results), at Richard's level of about 75 for a quality business with the concern clearing; it is held just below by one loose element and small current problems: the concern cannot fully clear before 2027 renewals and is the sector's to lift, and Region 3, the contractor reversal and the paused buyback blur it slightly.

Case Riskiness: 63, set by the Rater. The earnings risks are mostly paper cuts on simple, buffered operations with net cash and a multiple already near the bottom of its range (Richard's reasons on CVS Group), which lifts it a little above topic 9's 58, but the share price carries a sector-sentiment multiple that can fall 25-30% within weeks on others' news, as Richard weighed for Arteche at 60, and the lines below EBITDA are opaque with no guidance, so it sits in the low 60s, consistent with the memo's C.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
